Am I required to buy it?

Federal law requires it only in a high-risk zone (A or V) with a federally regulated or backed mortgage, or federal help to buy or build (42 U.S.C. §4012a). Outside those zones, a lender may still require it.

65.7% of Maine's NFIP policy units are in high-risk zones. That is a share of insured policy units, not of all buildings, and not an answer about your own home.

Of the NFIP claim dollars paid here (1978–2025), 26.2% went to claims rated outside high-risk zones A and V. That uses the zone on each claim, not today's map, and leaves out claims with no zone.

Policy records keep the code they were rated with, so older labels such as A1 to A30 are counted on their own. Every zone starting with A or V is high-risk; A1 to A30 and AE are the same kind of area (44 CFR §64.3).

Insured units by the zone each policy is rated in. How this is counted What each means: zone AE, zone X, zone VE. Find yours with the flood zone map lookup by address.

Not in the NFIP (29 communities here): Athens; Atkinson; Charleston; Columbia Falls; Crawford; Cutler; Dyer Brook; Frye Island; Gilead; Hersey; Lagrange; Marshfield; Moose River; Northfield; Parkman; Penobscot Indian Nation; Prospect; Shirley; Springfield; Talmadge; Tenpound Island; Two Bush Island; Vanceboro; Waldo; Wesley; Weston; Wheaton Island; Whiting; Whitneyville. Federal flood insurance (NFIP) is sold only in communities that take part in the NFIP; in a community that has not joined, or once a suspension takes effect, no one can buy an NFIP policy.

Flood insurance cost in Maine

In Maine, single-family primary-home NFIP policies typically cost about $981 a year ($82 a month), fees included. Half pay between $596 and $1,402. To check a quote, use the checker at the top.

A quarter pay under $596 · Typical $981 · A quarter pay over $1,402 · A tenth pay $2,403 or more

Each policy's annual cost (premium plus the federal policy fee, reserve fund assessment and HFIAA surcharge), single-family primary residences. The bar is the middle half of policies, from 2,693 single-family primary-home policies. These are existing policies, many still below FEMA's full-risk price.

The NFIP also offers policies for renters and businesses. The median here is for single-family primary-home policies, not businesses or second homes. Renting? See what renters pay.

Source: floodsmart.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

How do I actually get covered — and how fast?

Most policies start 30 days after you buy. Bought while making, increasing, extending or renewing a mortgage, it can start at closing if the insurer is paid within 10 days (30 if the lender, title company or settlement attorney pays).

  • Waiting period30 days
  • Bought with a new or refinanced mortgageCan start at closing, if paid in time
  • NFIP building limit$250,000
  • NFIP contents limit$100,000

Most homeowners insurance does not cover flood damage. Does homeowners insurance cover flooding? To buy: call the NFIP at (877) 336-2627, go to FloodSmart.gov, or ask any licensed insurance agent. Every NFIP insurer offers the same rates.

Already flooded? Insured: report the loss to your insurance agent or company now (FEMA's steps: how to start a flood claim), and send a proof of loss (your signed, sworn statement of the amount you are claiming) within 60 days of the flood (44 CFR 61, App. A(1), Art. VII). Not insured: a policy bought today will not cover a flood that already happened, and FEMA disaster aid is open to people in counties designated in a federally declared disaster.

Wait exceptions, exclusions, premium increases and surcharges, aid, appeals, rebuilding and closing rules: the NFIP rules in full.

Your state's insurance regulator: Maine Bureau of Insurance.

Source: floodsmart.gov, agents.floodsmart.gov, fema.gov, ecfr.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

Flood insurance claims in Maine: what floods pay out

Floods in Maine have led to 5,484 NFIP flood claims and $86.6 million in payouts since 1978; the worst years were 2024, 1987 and 2023.

Bar height is dollars paid that year. Orange bars are the three costliest years: 2024 ($29,242,015), 1987 ($10,142,203), 2023 ($8,199,125). Total paid $86,649,745. Totals for 2025 are not final while their claims stay open. How this is counted

Do flood claims here actually pay out?

Most do: 75.7% of claims in Maine paid something. The average paid claim was $20,940 (all years, in dollars of the day, not adjusted for inflation).

Typical claim: the median paid building claim was $6,500.

  • Average paid claim, incl. code-upgrade (ICC) pay$20,940
  • No recorded payment24.3%
  • Claims that paid4,150
Decade of the floodClaims filedShare that paid something
1970s69783.1%
1980s1,08675.0%
1990s1,26165.8%
2000s95578.2%
2010s43872.1%
2020s1,04782.5%

FEMA's claim records give a reason when a building claim has no recorded payment, such as damage less than the deductible, not an actual flood, seepage or backed-up drains. The average is over claims that paid something and includes Increased Cost of Compliance payments (help to elevate or rebuild to code), which the yearly totals above leave out. Dollars are as paid at the time, not adjusted for inflation; a single home can file across several floods over the years. All years, records FEMA coded as entered in error left out (the claims page uses losses from 2020 on, so its shares differ). FEMA's data has no open or closed field, so a recent claim with no payment may still be paid.

Would a policy here pay to rebuild my home?

Not in full for at least 46.7% of the 1,321 single-family policies here that report a rebuilding cost: FEMA's records put it above the NFIP's $250,000 building limit.

  • Rebuilding cost above the building limit (of 1,321 policies reporting one)46.7%
  • Single-family policies insured to the building maximum (all of them, not only those above)72.0%
  • Damage was more than the coverage (of 3,963 claims paid with a damage figure)5.0%

The two shares have different bases: insured-to-the-maximum counts every single-family policy with the full building limit; the rebuilding-cost share counts only the policies that report a rebuilding cost. Homes insured for less than their own rebuilding cost can also fall short. How this is counted

The NFIP pays the cost to rebuild (not a depreciated value) only for a single-family home that is your principal residence and is insured for at least 80% of its full rebuilding cost, or for the $250,000 maximum.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Policies; FEMA OpenFEMA — NFIP Claims. Data effective August 31, 2026; retrieved November 14, 2026.

What does it cost in my flood zone?

From about $670 a year (Zone X) to $1,447 (Zone VE) here. Your zone is on your lender's flood determination or FEMA's map; find its row below.

Flood zoneMedian / yrPriced policies
Zone X$6701,103
Zone AE$1,2311,073
Zone A$872214
Zone C$1,036116
Zone VE$1,447115

What the zone codes mean (44 CFR §64.3): A, AE and A1–A30 are high-risk; AO and AH are high-risk with shallow flooding; A99 is high-risk behind a flood barrier FEMA treats as complete; V, VE and V1–V30 are coastal high-risk, flooded by tides with fast-moving water (velocity); B and X are areas of moderate flood hazard, C and X areas of minimal hazard; D has possible but undetermined flood hazards. A 1 percent or greater chance a year works out to a 26% or greater chance of at least one such flood over 30 years.

Zones with fewer than 50 priced single-family policies are omitted. Your own premium still depends on elevation and coverage.

Source: ecfr.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

Why do sites quote different prices for Maine?

Because they measure different things. Existing single-family policies here typically cost $981 a year, and policies first bought in the past year $835; other sites count other policies, years or averages.

MeasureAmountWhat it counts
Typical cost, single-family homes (median)$981premium plus fees; the middle policy
Typical premium only$770before the federal fee, reserve fund and surcharge
Typical cost, policies whose term began Jan–Aug 2026$9761,589 policies
Typical cost, policies first bought in the past year$835200 policies, past year
FEMA's full-risk premium (median)$860the price FEMA's model sets for these existing policies
Full-risk premium plus average fees$1,115what these existing policies would cost at FEMA's full price
Average (mean) cost, single-family homes$1,270pulled up by a few expensive policies
Average cost, every policy type$2,051adds condos, rentals and businesses

Condo owners: condo-unit policies are 3.6% of NFIP policy units here and whole condo buildings 0.9%. The every-policy-type average includes them. Condo-unit policies here have a median cost of $941 a year (premium plus fees, 311 priced policies; condo flood insurance by state). The single-family figures leave out every policy FEMA marks as a condo unit or a whole condo building.

All from the NFIP policies in force on August 31, 2026. How this is counted

How do current premiums compare with FEMA's full-risk price?

42.0% of single-family primary-home policies in Maine have a premium below FEMA's full-risk premium by any amount (not a quote). Median premium $770, full-risk $860 (premiums only, before fees).

  • Median premium charged (before fees)$770
  • Median full-risk premium$860
  • Pay below full-risk42.0% of 2,693

Yearly cap: By law, most premium rates may not rise more than 18% a year (42 U.S.C. §4015(e)).

Source: agents.floodsmart.gov, govinfo.gov (official pages, checked October 25, 2026). Not endorsed by FEMA.

How Maine appears in the national research papers

Each paper sorts the U.S. counties with enough records by one measure into five groups of about equal size, from highest fifth to lowest fifth. A group is a position in a list, not a grade or a prediction.

  • Flood damage over building coverage: NFIP claims by county: 1 of this state's counties have at least 100 paid single-family primary-home claims with recorded damage and coverage and are listed.
  • Outside the zone: paid flood claims rated outside high-risk zones: 1 of this state's counties have at least 100 claims with a payment and a rated zone and are listed.
  • Building deductibles on record: NFIP single-family homes by county: 15 of this state's counties have at least 30 single-family primary-home policy units with a known building deductible and are listed.
  • Peak month of NFIP claims by county: 2 of this state's counties have at least 100 NFIP claims with a month of loss and are listed.
  • The gap to FEMA's full-risk premium: NFIP single-family homes by county: 15 of this state's counties have at least 30 single-family primary-home policies priced both ways and are listed.

Can I pay less?

The usual building deductible here is $1,250 (39.2% of single-family policies). FEMA's ways that may lower an NFIP bill: a higher deductible (you pay more of any loss), work that lowers the building's flood risk, and an Elevation Certificate.

Do the same homes flood again here?

Yes: FEMA's disaster-aid records hold 239 records from homes here that FEMA lists as flood-damaged in more than one declared disaster.

  • Disaster-aid records on repeat-flood homes239

These count records, one per home per declared disaster, not distinct homes, and FEMA does not mark flood damage on every record. How this is counted

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Individual Assistance Multiple-Loss Flood Properties. Data: FEMA's current multiple-loss list; retrieved November 14, 2026.

How often is Maine a flood disaster?

46 federal disasters for floods or storms here; the latest was Severe Storms and Flooding (2024).

  • March 2024 — Severe Storms and Flooding
  • January 2024 — Severe Storm and Flooding
  • September 2023 — Hurricane Lee (emergency declaration)
  • September 2023 — Severe Storm and Flooding (two separate declarations)
  • July 2023 — Severe Storm and Flooding

Only the latest are listed, newest first. Disasters with the same month and title share one line, which says how many. The count covers every flood, hurricane, tropical-storm and coastal-storm declaration FEMA lists here, plus severe-storm declarations whose title names flooding, including emergency declarations. How this is counted

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Disaster Declarations Summaries. Data: declarations through 2024; retrieved November 14, 2026.

Did FEMA aid homeowners after floods and storms?

Yes: FEMA approved $15.7 million for homeowners here after floods and storms, about $1,954 per registration.

FEMA disaster aid helps with uninsured and underinsured losses, and is separate from NFIP insurance. The average is over every registration, including those approved for nothing. Only disasters counted in the flood-disaster card are included; their aid can still cover wind or tornado damage from the same storm. Disasters for COVID, fire, winter storms or tornadoes alone are left out.

Source: FEMA OpenFEMA — Housing Assistance (Owners). Data: homeowner aid by disaster; retrieved November 14, 2026.

Every record FEMA's download lists was received and counted.
